R = N_A k_B = 8.31 J/(mol · K)

e = 1.602 × 10^{−19} C
1 eV = 1.602 × 10^{−19} J
h = 6.63 × 10^{−34} J · s = 4.14 × 10^{−15} eV · s
m_e = 9.109 × 10^{−31} kg = 0.511 MeV/c^2

**Useful Approximations**
(1 + x)^n ≈ 1 + nx + n(n − 1)x^2/2 for |nx| ≪ 1
e^x ≈ 1 + x + x^2/2 + x^3/6 for |x| ≪ 1
sin θ ≈ θ − θ^3/6 for |θ| ≪ 1
cos θ ≈ 1 − θ^2/2 for |θ| ≪ 1

**Useful Identities**
\sum_{k=0}^N \cos(ka + \phi) = \frac{\sin(\frac{(N+1)a}{2}) \cdot \cos(\frac{Na}{2} + \phi)}{\sin(\frac{a}{2})}
\sum_{k=0}^N \sin(ka + \phi) = \frac{\sin(\frac{(N+1)a}{2}) \cdot \sin(\frac{Na}{2} + \phi)}{\sin(\frac{a}{2})}
\sum_{k=1}^N \cos^2(ka) = \frac{N}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=1}^N \cos(2ka)
\sum_{k=1}^N \sin^2(ka) = \frac{N}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=1}^N \cos(2ka)

**Problem A1: Shake It**
Most hairy mammals shake after getting wet; shaking the water off is energetically advantageous to waiting for it to dry on its own. In this problem, we investigate the mechanics of shaking off water. For simplicity, we will model animals as solid cylinders with the sides covered in fur. You may ignore gravity throughout the problem.

a. We can model the shaking by assuming that the angular position of the cylinder undergoes a sinusoidal oscillation: θ = A cos(ωt). (The rotation is about the axis of rotational symmetry.) Letting the radius of the cylindrical animal be R, derive an expression for the magnitude of the acceleration of a point on the surface of the animal under such a motion.

b. For the rest of this problem, rather than modeling sinusoidal motion, we will assume that the cylindrical animal is simply spinning at constant angular speed ω. Wet fur tends to separate into cylindrical clumps of radius r ≪ R. A droplet of water on the end of a clump of fur will be separated from it if the centripetal force overcomes the forces due to surface tension. Derive an approximate relationship (valid up to scalar numerical constants) between the surface tension σ, the radius r of the fur clump, the radius R of the animal, the angular speed ω, and the density ρ of water. The diagram below show the cross-section of the animal, showing four clumps of fur with droplets on their end.
[Diagram description: A large circle representing the cross-section of the cylindrical animal. On the right side of the circle, four small, closely spaced cylindrical clumps of fur protrude radially outward. Each clump has a small hemispherical droplet of water at its outer end.]

c. Experimentally, it is observed that all mammalian fur forms clumps of similar radius. Under the assumption that different animals all have the same density and are simply scaled copies of each other (i.e. larger animals are both longer and fatter), the relationship between an animal’s mass M and its angular velocity of shaking ω is of the form ω ∼ M^n: find the value of n.

d. Shaking requires energy, which we can crudely model as the rotational energy of the corresponding cylinder. An alternative strategy for the animal is to simply air-dry their fur, which requires energy to evaporate the water. Assume a wet animal has approximately 5% of their body weight in water, and has to supply all the energy for evaporating the water. Our model predicts that for some animal sizes, it will be energetically advantageous to air dry themselves: estimate the range of animal masses for which this is true. You may use the following facts: a mouse weighs 20 g, has a radius of 1 cm, and shakes itself with angular velocity ω = 30 rad/s. The latent heat of vaporization of water at room temperature is λ = 2430 J/g.

turns.official_answer:
a. ARω^2 \sqrt{A^2 \sin^4(ωt) + \cos^2(ωt)}
b. ω^2 ∼ \frac{σr}{ρr^3 R} (or ω ∼ \sqrt{\frac{σ}{ρr^2 R}})
c. n = -1/6
d. M ≳ 3 × 10^{18} kg

turns.candidate_answer:
### a. Acceleration for sinusoidal angular motion

For a point on the surface, its distance from the rotation axis is \(R\). With

\[
\theta=A\cos(\omega t),
\]

the angular velocity and angular acceleration are

\[
\dot\theta=-A\omega \sin(\omega t),
\qquad
\ddot\theta=-A\omega^2\cos(\omega t).
\]

The surface point has radial centripetal acceleration \(R\dot\theta^2\) and tangential acceleration \(R\ddot\theta\), which are perpendicular. Thus

\[
a=R\sqrt{\dot\theta^4+\ddot\theta^2}.
\]

Substituting,

\[
\boxed{
a(t)=R A\omega^2\sqrt{\cos^2(\omega t)+A^2\sin^4(\omega t)}
}
\]

For small angular amplitude \(A\ll 1\), this is approximately

\[
a(t)\approx R A\omega^2|\cos(\omega t)|.
\]

---

### b. Detachment condition for a droplet

A droplet on the end of a fur clump has characteristic radius \(r\), so its mass scales as

\[
m\sim \rho r^3.
\]

The centripetal force needed to keep it moving with the animal is

\[
F_c\sim m R\omega^2 \sim \rho r^3 R\omega^2.
\]

Surface tension holds the droplet on with a force of order surface tension times contact perimeter:

\[
F_\sigma \sim \sigma r.
\]

Detachment occurs when these are comparable:

\[
\rho r^3 R\omega^2 \sim \sigma r.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
R\omega^2 \sim \frac{\sigma}{\rho r^2}
}
\]

or equivalently

\[
\boxed{
\omega^2 \sim \frac{\sigma}{\rho r^2 R}.
}
\]

---

### c. Scaling of shaking angular velocity with mass

If all animals have similar fur clump radius \(r\), and water has the same \(\rho\) and \(\sigma\), then from part b,

\[
\omega^2 \propto \frac{1}{R},
\]

so

\[
\omega \propto R^{-1/2}.
\]

For geometrically similar animals of the same density,

\[
M\propto R^3,
\]

so

\[
R\propto M^{1/3}.
\]

Thus

\[
\omega \propto M^{-1/6}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{n=-\frac16}.
\]

---

### d. Mass range where air-drying is energetically favorable

For a solid cylinder,

\[
I=\frac12 MR^2,
\]

so the rotational energy is

\[
E_{\text{shake}}\sim \frac12 I\omega^2
=\frac14 MR^2\omega^2.
\]

Using the mouse data:

\[
M_0=20\text{ g}=0.020\text{ kg},\qquad R_0=0.010\text{ m},\qquad \omega_0=30\text{ rad/s}.
\]

So

\[
E_{\text{shake},0}
=\frac14(0.020)(0.010)^2(30)^2
\approx 4.5\times 10^{-4}\text{ J}.
\]

The mouse carries about \(5\%\) of its body mass in water, so water mass is

\[
0.05(20\text{ g})=1\text{ g}.
\]

Thus the evaporation energy is

\[
E_{\text{evap},0}=1\text{ g}\times 2430\text{ J/g}
=2.43\times 10^3\text{ J}.
\]

For scaled animals,

\[
R\propto M^{1/3},
\qquad
\omega\propto M^{-1/6}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
E_{\text{shake}}\propto MR^2\omega^2
\propto M\cdot M^{2/3}\cdot M^{-1/3}
= M^{4/3}.
\]

Meanwhile,

\[
E_{\text{evap}}\propto M.
\]

Let

\[
x=\frac{M}{M_0}.
\]

Then

\[
E_{\text{shake}}=4.5\times 10^{-4}x^{4/3},
\]

and

\[
E_{\text{evap}}=2.43\times 10^3 x.
\]

Air-drying is favorable when

\[
E_{\text{evap}}<E_{\text{shake}}.
\]

Set them equal:

\[
4.5\times 10^{-4}x^{4/3}=2.43\times 10^3 x.
\]

Thus

\[
x^{1/3}\approx \frac{2.43\times 10^3}{4.5\times 10^{-4}}
\approx 5.4\times 10^6,
\]

so

\[
x\approx (5.4\times 10^6)^3\approx 1.6\times 10^{20}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
M\approx (20\text{ g})(1.6\times 10^{20})
\approx 3\times 10^{21}\text{ g}
=3\times 10^{18}\text{ kg}.
\]

So the model predicts air-drying is energetically favorable only for

\[
\boxed{M\gtrsim 10^{18}\text{ kg}}
\]

more specifically around

\[
\boxed{M\gtrsim 3\times 10^{18}\text{ kg}.}
\]

This is far larger than any real mammal, so for ordinary animals shaking is vastly more energetically favorable.

turns.question:
Problem A2: Black Tides

Consider a spherically symmetric, nonrotating star of mass $m$ and radius $r$. If it gets too close to the supermassive black hole of mass $M \gg m$ at the center of a galaxy, it will be ripped apart by tidal forces. Throughout this problem, neglect relativistic effects and give answers in terms of $G$, $M$, $m$, and $r$. When asked for numbers, assume the star is Sun-like, so that $m = 2 \times 10^{30} \text{ kg}$, $r = 7 \times 10^8 \text{ m}$, and $M = 10^6 m$, and give all numeric answers to one significant figure.

a. Suppose the star orbits the black hole in a circle of radius $R$. What is the radius of curvature of the trajectory of each point on the star's surface? Note that the star does not rotate as it orbits.

b. Gas on the star's surface facing the black hole is attracted to the star by the star's gravity, and pulled away from the star by the black hole's tidal force. Write an expression for the tidal acceleration at the point closest to the black hole.

c. At a radius $R$ where the gravitational and tidal forces are in equilibrium, the star will start being tidally ripped apart. This effect can only be observed when $R$ is outside the black hole's Schwarzschild radius $R_s = 2GM/c^2$. Find an expression for $R$ and numerically evaluate the ratio $R/R_s$.

For the rest of the problem, we consider a star on a parabolic orbit whose periapsis (distance of closest approach) is equal to the radius $R$ found in part c. Near periapsis, the star will be torn apart in a “tidal disruption event”. As a very rough model of this phenomenon, assume the star is initially a single rigid body. The moment it reaches periapsis, it fragments into many rigid pieces which do not interact with other, and feel only the black hole's gravity.

d. Afterward, some of the fragments will escape from the black hole, while the rest remain bound. Numerically evaluate the fraction of the mass which escapes.

e. An escaping fragment has speed $v_f$ when it is far from the black hole. Find the maximum possible value of $v_f$, among all fragments, and evaluate it numerically.

f. A bound fragment orbits with period $T_f$. Find the minimum possible value of $T_f$, among all fragments, and evaluate it numerically.

As bound fragments return to the location of the initial disruption, they collide with other debris, causing them to be absorbed into the black hole's accretion disk. This process produces an enormous amount of light, with the luminosity (or energy emitted over time) proportional to the mass absorption rate. If $t = 0$ at the moment the star fragments apart, then light begins to be emitted at the time you found in part f, and afterward the luminosity scales as $L \propto 1/t^n$ for a constant $n$.

g. Find the value of $n$. Assume for simplicity that the total energies of the bound fragments are uniformly distributed between their minimum and maximum values.
turns.official_answer:
a. $R$
b. $\frac{2GMr}{R^3}$
c. $R = r\left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/3}$, $R/R_s = 30$
d. $0.5$
e. $v_f = \left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/6} \sqrt{\frac{Gm}{r}} = 5 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}$
f. $T_f = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{r^3}{2Gm}} \sqrt{\frac{M}{m}} = 7 \times 10^6 \text{ s} = 80 \text{ days}$
g. $n = 5/3$

turns.candidate_answer:
## a. Radius of curvature of surface-point trajectories

Since the star does **not** rotate as it orbits, every point on the star has the same translational circular motion as the center of the star, just shifted by a fixed vector.

Thus every surface point traces out a circle with radius of curvature

\[
\boxed{R}
\]

not \(R-r\) or \(R+r\).

---

## b. Tidal acceleration at the point closest to the black hole

The center of the star has gravitational acceleration

\[
a_{\rm center}=\frac{GM}{R^2}.
\]

The surface point closest to the black hole is at distance \(R-r\), so the black hole pulls it with acceleration

\[
a_{\rm near}=\frac{GM}{(R-r)^2}.
\]

Therefore the tidal acceleration pulling the gas away from the star is

\[
\boxed{
a_{\rm tide}=\frac{GM}{(R-r)^2}-\frac{GM}{R^2}
}
\]

For \(r\ll R\),

\[
\boxed{
a_{\rm tide}\approx \frac{2GMr}{R^3}
}
\]

where \(M\) is the black hole mass.

---

## c. Tidal disruption radius and comparison with Schwarzschild radius

The surface gravity of the star is

\[
a_{\rm star}=\frac{Gm}{r^2}.
\]

Tidal disruption begins when

\[
\frac{Gm}{r^2}\sim \frac{2GMr}{R^3}.
\]

Thus

\[
R^3 \sim \frac{2Mr^3}{m},
\]

so

\[
\boxed{
R \approx r\left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/3}
}
\]

For \(M=10^6m\),

\[
R\approx (7\times 10^8)\left(2\times 10^6\right)^{1/3}
\approx 9\times 10^{10}\ \text{m}.
\]

The Schwarzschild radius is

\[
R_s=\frac{2GM}{c^2}.
\]

For \(M=10^6m=2\times 10^{36}\ \text{kg}\),

\[
R_s\approx 3\times 10^9\ \text{m}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\frac{R}{R_s}\approx 3\times 10^1
}
\]

so the disruption occurs well outside the Schwarzschild radius.

---

For the remaining parts, the center of the star is on a parabolic orbit, so at periapsis

\[
v_p=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}.
\]

A fragment at distance \(D\) from the black hole has specific orbital energy

\[
\varepsilon=\frac12 v_p^2-\frac{GM}{D}
=\frac{GM}{R}-\frac{GM}{D}.
\]

For a displacement \(x\) from the star’s center, positive away from the black hole,

\[
D\approx R+x,
\]

so

\[
\varepsilon\approx \frac{GMx}{R^2}.
\]

---

## d. Fraction of mass that escapes

Fragments with

\[
\varepsilon>0
\]

escape. Since \(\varepsilon\propto x\), the fragments on the half of the star farther from the black hole escape, while the closer half remains bound.

Thus

\[
\boxed{
f_{\rm esc}\approx \frac12
}
\]

Numerically,

\[
\boxed{f_{\rm esc}\approx 0.5}
\]

---

## e. Maximum escaping speed far from the black hole

The largest positive energy belongs to the farthest fragment, with \(x=r\). Thus

\[
\varepsilon_{\max}\approx \frac{GMr}{R^2}.
\]

At infinity,

\[
\varepsilon_{\max}=\frac12 v_{f,\max}^2,
\]

so

\[
v_{f,\max}\approx \sqrt{\frac{2GMr}{R^2}}.
\]

Using

\[
R=r\left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/3},
\]

this can also be written as

\[
\boxed{
v_{f,\max}\approx
\left(2^{1/3}\frac{G M^{1/3}m^{2/3}}{r}\right)^{1/2}
}
\]

Numerically,

\[
\boxed{
v_{f,\max}\approx 5\times 10^6\ \text{m/s}
}
\]

---

## f. Minimum period of a bound fragment

The most bound fragment has

\[
\varepsilon_{\min}\approx -\frac{GMr}{R^2}.
\]

For a Keplerian orbit,

\[
\varepsilon=-\frac{GM}{2a},
\]

so for the most bound fragment,

\[
a_{\min}\approx \frac{R^2}{2r}.
\]

Then

\[
T_{\min}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{a_{\min}^3}{GM}}.
\]

Substituting,

\[
T_{\min}
\approx
\frac{2\pi GM}{\left(2GMr/R^2\right)^{3/2}}.
\]

Using \(R^3=2Mr^3/m\),

\[
\boxed{
T_{\min}\approx \pi\sqrt{\frac{2Mr^3}{Gm^2}}
}
\]

Numerically,

\[
\boxed{
T_{\min}\approx 7\times 10^6\ \text{s}
}
\]

which is about \(80\) days.

---

## g. Luminosity power-law exponent

For bound fragments,

\[
T\propto |\varepsilon|^{-3/2}.
\]

Thus

\[
|\varepsilon|\propto T^{-2/3}.
\]

If the fragment mass is uniformly distributed in energy, then

\[
\frac{dM}{d\varepsilon}=\text{constant}.
\]

The mass return rate is

\[
\frac{dM}{dt}
=
\frac{dM}{d\varepsilon}\left|\frac{d\varepsilon}{dt}\right|
\propto t^{-5/3}.
\]

Since luminosity is proportional to the mass absorption rate,

\[
L\propto t^{-5/3}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
n=\frac53
}
\]

turns.question:
In this problem, we explore some of the design considerations for an electromagnet.

**a.** Consider an electromagnet consisting of a long solenoid, i.e. a spiral of thin wire wrapped in a single layer around a cylindrical nonmagnetic core. The wire is wrapped in such a way that the adjacent coils almost touch. When a current is sent through the wire, a magnetic field is generated inside the solenoid; this magnetic field exerts an outward force on the wire. Find the pressure $P$ on the solenoid in terms of the magnetic field $B$ inside the solenoid.

**b.** The pressure on the "walls" of the solenoid is counteracted by tension inside the wire. Derive an expression for the maximal achievable magnetic field $B$ in terms of coil radius $a$, wire diameter (thickness) $t \ll a$, and wire tensile strength $\sigma$. (The tensile strength of a material is the force per unit cross-sectional area that needs to be applied in order to pull the material apart.) Assume the wire is circular in cross-section.

**c.** Let $a = 0.1\text{ m}$, $t = 0.001\text{ m}$. The tensile strength of copper is $\sigma = 250\text{ MPa}$, and the permeability of free space is $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ H/m}$. What is the maximum magnetic field that can be achieved in a single-layer solenoid made out of such a wire without the wire snapping?

**d.** In theory, we could generate a stronger field by increasing the wire thickness, but the nonuniform distribution of current inside the wire makes this difficult to analyze.
Instead, consider wrapping the solenoid in many layers of wire. We will place adjacent layers a distance $t$ apart so that they just barely don't touch, and will adjust the current through each wire to equalize the tensile stress. The wire coils span the space from an inner core radius of $a$ to an outer radius of $b$. Estimate the maximum achievable field strength inside this electromagnet. You may assume that the wire is thin ($t \ll a$, $t \ll b - a$).

**e.** Estimate the numeric value of the maximum magnetic field that can be achieved in a multi-layer solenoid described above with $a = 0.1\text{ m}$ and $b = 0.3\text{ m}$.
turns.official_rubric:
**Part a (5 points)**
- [2 points] Relating pressure to energy density or force per unit area.
- [3 points] Correct expression $P = B^2/(2\mu_0)$.

**Part b (6 points)**
- [2 points] Relating outward force to tension (e.g., $F_{\text{out}} = P \cdot t \cdot a \cdot d\theta$).
- [2 points] Expressing tension in terms of tensile strength ($T = \frac{\pi}{4} t^2 \sigma$).
- [2 points] Correct final expression for $B$.

**Part c (3 points)**
- [3 points] Correct numerical value $2.2\text{ T}$.

**Part d (8 points)**
- [2 points] Identifying the field difference or energy density difference across a single layer $k$.
- [2 points] Setting up the constraint $B_k^2 - B_{k-1}^2 \le \frac{\pi}{2} \sigma \mu_0 \frac{t}{r_k}$.
- [2 points] Summing over all layers or setting up the corresponding integral.
- [2 points] Correct final expression $B \le \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2} \sigma \mu_0 \ln(b/a)}$.

**Part e (3 points)**
- [3 points] Correct numerical value $23.3\text{ T}$.

turns.candidate_answer:
## a. Magnetic pressure on a solenoid

For a long solenoid, the magnetic field is approximately \(B\) inside and approximately zero outside.

The magnetic energy density is

\[
u=\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}.
\]

Equivalently, the field exerts an outward magnetic pressure of this same magnitude on the solenoid walls:

\[
\boxed{P=\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}}.
\]

---

## b. Maximum field for a single-layer solenoid

Consider one circular turn of wire of radius \(a\). The wire diameter is \(t\), and adjacent turns are separated by approximately \(t\), so one turn supports pressure over an axial width \(\sim t\).

The outward force on a small arc subtending angle \(d\phi\) is

\[
dF=P(a\,d\phi)t.
\]

The inward force supplied by wire tension \(T\) is approximately

\[
dF_T=T\,d\phi.
\]

Thus

\[
T=P a t.
\]

The wire snaps when

\[
T=\sigma A_{\text{wire}},
\]

where

\[
A_{\text{wire}}=\frac{\pi t^2}{4}.
\]

Therefore

\[
P_{\max}a t=\sigma \frac{\pi t^2}{4},
\]

so

\[
P_{\max}=\frac{\pi\sigma t}{4a}.
\]

Using

\[
P=\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0},
\]

we get

\[
\frac{B_{\max}^2}{2\mu_0}=\frac{\pi\sigma t}{4a}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
B_{\max}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi\mu_0\sigma t}{2a}}
}.
\]

---

## c. Numerical value for copper single-layer solenoid

Given

\[
a=0.1\text{ m},\qquad t=0.001\text{ m},\qquad \sigma=250\text{ MPa}=2.5\times10^8\text{ Pa},
\]

and

\[
\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\text{ H/m},
\]

\[
B_{\max}
=
\sqrt{\frac{\pi(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.5\times10^8)(10^{-3})}{2(0.1)}}.
\]

This gives

\[
B_{\max}\approx 2.2\text{ T}.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{B_{\max}\approx 2\text{ T}}.
\]

---

## d. Maximum field for a multilayer solenoid

Now suppose the solenoid has many layers from radius \(a\) to radius \(b\). Consider one layer at radius \(\rho\).

As in part b, the maximum magnetic pressure that this layer can withstand is

\[
P_{\max}(\rho)=\frac{\pi\sigma t}{4\rho}.
\]

Let \(B_{\rm in}\) and \(B_{\rm out}\) be the magnetic fields just inside and just outside that layer. The magnetic pressure on that layer is

\[
P=\frac{B_{\rm in}^2-B_{\rm out}^2}{2\mu_0}.
\]

At maximum field, each layer is stressed to its tensile limit, so

\[
\frac{B_{\rm in}^2-B_{\rm out}^2}{2\mu_0}
=
\frac{\pi\sigma t}{4\rho}.
\]

Since the layers are separated by approximately \(t\), summing from \(a\) to \(b\) gives

\[
\frac{B_{\max}^2}{2\mu_0}
\approx
\int_a^b \frac{1}{t}\frac{\pi\sigma t}{4\rho}\,d\rho.
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{B_{\max}^2}{2\mu_0}
=
\frac{\pi\sigma}{4}\ln\left(\frac{b}{a}\right).
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
B_{\max}
\approx
\sqrt{
\frac{\pi\mu_0\sigma}{2}
\ln\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)
}
}.
\]

Notably, in this approximation the wire thickness \(t\) cancels out.

---

## e. Numerical value for \(a=0.1\text{ m}\), \(b=0.3\text{ m}\)

Using

\[
\ln\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)=\ln 3\approx 1.10,
\]

\[
B_{\max}
=
\sqrt{
\frac{\pi(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.5\times10^8)}{2}
\ln 3
}.
\]

This gives

\[
B_{\max}\approx 23\text{ T}.
\]

So the multilayer solenoid can reach roughly

\[
\boxed{B_{\max}\approx 2\times 10^1\text{ T}}
\]

or about

\[
\boxed{20\text{--}25\text{ T}}.
\]

Problem B1: Scroll 'n' Roll

Consider a disk with mass $m$ and radius $R$ placed on a large and frictionless table. An ant with mass $m$ is placed on top of the disk. The ant can move freely without sliding on the disk.

a. Initially, the ant starts on the edge of the disk, and both the ant and the disk are at rest (relative to the table). Then, the ant starts walking across the disk's diameter, such that in the frame of the disk, the ant has (constant) velocity $v$. What is ant's velocity in the frame of the table?

b. Suppose instead that the ant walks counterclockwise along the edge of the disk at constant speed $v$ in the frame of the disk. What is the ant's speed in the frame of the table?

c. Now there are two ants on the disk! The second ant (also of mass $m$) starts at distance $R/2$ from the center of the disk, with an angle offset by $\theta$ from the first ant. The second ant walks counterclockwise around this circle with radius $R/2$ at speed $v/2$ (relative to the disk). Find all $\theta$ such that the second ant is stationary in the frame of the table.

turns.candidate_answer:
Let the disk’s center have velocity \(\mathbf V\). Since the table is frictionless, total horizontal momentum is conserved. Initially it is zero.

The disk has moment of inertia

\[
I=\frac12 mR^2.
\]

---

## a. Ant walking across a diameter

The ant walks along a diameter with velocity \(\mathbf v\) relative to the disk. Since the ant’s position and relative velocity are along the same diameter, there is no angular momentum generated about the disk center, so the disk does not rotate.

Thus the ant’s table-frame velocity is

\[
\mathbf u=\mathbf V+\mathbf v.
\]

Momentum conservation gives

\[
m\mathbf V+m\mathbf u=0.
\]

Substitute \(\mathbf u=\mathbf V+\mathbf v\):

\[
m\mathbf V+m(\mathbf V+\mathbf v)=0,
\]

so

\[
2\mathbf V=-\mathbf v.
\]

Therefore

\[
\mathbf u=\mathbf V+\mathbf v=\frac{\mathbf v}{2}.
\]

So the ant moves in the table frame with velocity

\[
\boxed{\mathbf u=\frac{\mathbf v}{2}}
\]

along the same diameter.

---

## b. Ant walking around the edge

Let the disk rotate with angular velocity \(\Omega\), positive counterclockwise. The ant walks counterclockwise relative to the disk with angular speed

\[
\frac{v}{R}.
\]

Therefore the angular speed of the ant’s position relative to the disk center in the table frame is

\[
\Omega+\frac{v}{R}.
\]

The ant’s velocity relative to the disk center has magnitude

\[
w=R\left(\Omega+\frac{v}{R}\right)=R\Omega+v.
\]

Since the disk and ant have equal mass, momentum conservation gives the ant’s table-frame speed as

\[
u=\frac{w}{2}.
\]

Now use angular momentum conservation. About the center of mass of the disk-ant system,

\[
0=I\Omega+\frac{m}{2}R^2\left(\Omega+\frac{v}{R}\right).
\]

Using \(I=\frac12 mR^2\),

\[
0=\frac12 mR^2\Omega+\frac12 mR^2\left(\Omega+\frac{v}{R}\right).
\]

Thus

\[
2\Omega+\frac{v}{R}=0,
\]

so

\[
\Omega=-\frac{v}{2R}.
\]

Then

\[
w=R\left(-\frac{v}{2R}+\frac{v}{R}\right)=\frac v2.
\]

Therefore the ant’s speed in the table frame is

\[
\boxed{u=\frac v4}.
\]

---

## c. Two ants

Let the first ant be on the rim, and let the second ant be at radius \(R/2\), angularly offset by \(\theta\). Both ants have the same angular speed relative to the disk:

\[
\frac{v}{R}=\frac{v/2}{R/2}.
\]

Let

\[
n=\frac{v}{R}.
\]

If the disk has angular velocity \(\Omega\), define

\[
K=\Omega+n.
\]

Then the velocities of the ants relative to the disk center in the table frame are

\[
\mathbf w_1=KR\hat{\mathbf t}_1,
\]

\[
\mathbf w_2=K\frac R2\hat{\mathbf t}_2,
\]

where \(\hat{\mathbf t}_1\) and \(\hat{\mathbf t}_2\) are the tangential unit vectors of the first and second ants.

Momentum conservation for the disk plus two ants gives

\[
m\mathbf V+m(\mathbf V+\mathbf w_1)+m(\mathbf V+\mathbf w_2)=0,
\]

so

\[
\mathbf V=-\frac{\mathbf w_1+\mathbf w_2}{3}.
\]

The second ant’s table-frame velocity is therefore

\[
\mathbf u_2=\mathbf V+\mathbf w_2
=\frac{2\mathbf w_2-\mathbf w_1}{3}.
\]

Substitute \(\mathbf w_1\) and \(\mathbf w_2\):

\[
\mathbf u_2
=
\frac{KR}{3}\left(\hat{\mathbf t}_2-\hat{\mathbf t}_1\right).
\]

So \(\mathbf u_2=0\) requires either \(K=0\) or

\[
\hat{\mathbf t}_2=\hat{\mathbf t}_1.
\]

But \(K\neq 0\). Indeed, angular momentum conservation gives

\[
K=\frac{3n}{2(4-\cos\theta)},
\]

which is nonzero for all \(\theta\).

Thus we need

\[
\hat{\mathbf t}_2=\hat{\mathbf t}_1,
\]

meaning the two ants must lie on the same radial line. Therefore

\[
\boxed{\theta=0 \pmod{2\pi}}.
\]

If \(\theta\) is restricted to \(0\le \theta<2\pi\), then

\[
\boxed{\theta=0}.
\]

turns.question:
Problem B2: Where's the Kaboom?

A plane is flying horizontally at constant velocity $v$ and altitude $z = H$. The speed of sound at altitude $z$ is given by
$$c(z) = \alpha \sqrt{T(z)},$$
where $\alpha$ is a constant. Suppose $v > c(H)$, and define the Mach number as
$$M \equiv \frac{v}{c(H)} > 1.$$
If $c(z)$ is constant for all $z$, then the envelope is a cone with half angle $\theta$ where $\sin \theta = \frac{1}{M}$ and propagates with the speed of sound $c$.

a. Sketch the envelope.

b. Now, the speed of sound depends on the altitude because the temperature is not uniform. For the altitudes we are interested in, the following linear model works well:
$$T(z) = T_0 - \beta z,$$
where $\beta > 0$ is a constant. Sketch the envelope of the boom.

c. If the Mach number is large enough then the sonic boom hits the ground. Assume it is large enough. On the ground, there are two sensors at $z = 0$ and $z = h$, one directly above the other. Assume $h \ll H$ and $\beta h \ll T_0$. At time $t_1$, the top sensor receives the sonic boom signal and at a later time, the bottom sensor also receives the signal. Express the Mach number $M$ of the airplane in terms of $H, h, t, T_0, \alpha, \beta$, where $t = t_2 - t_1$.

d. If the plane travels slower without changing direction, its sonic boom could become no longer audible from the ground for the Mach number $1 < M < M_{\text{max}}$. What is the upper limit for the Mach number $M_{\text{max}}$ for which this can occur? Express your answer in terms of $T_0, H, \alpha, \beta$. You do not necessarily need all of these parameters.
turns.official_answer:
a. A sketch showing a straight cone originating from the plane with half-angle $\theta$ such that $\sin \theta = 1/M$.

b. A sketch showing the sonic boom envelope as a curve that becomes less steep (bends outwards, increasing the angle with the horizontal) as it approaches the ground.

c. $M = \left[ \left(1 - \frac{\beta H}{T_0}\right) \left(1 - \frac{\alpha^2 t^2 T_0}{h^2}\right) \right]^{-1/2}$

d. $M_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{T_0}{T_0 - \beta H}}$

- 2 points for correctly indicating the half-angle $\theta$ between the plane's path and the envelope, consistent with $\sin \theta = 1/M$.

Part b (6 points):
- 2 points for recognizing that the speed of sound $c(z)$ increases as altitude $z$ decreases (since temperature $T(z)$ increases).
- 2 points for applying Snell's law ($\sin \theta / c = \text{const}$) or equivalent reasoning to deduce that the angle $\theta$ increases at lower altitudes.
- 2 points for sketching a curved envelope that becomes less steep (more horizontal, larger $\theta$) as it approaches the ground.

Part c (10 points):
- 2 points for relating the local angle at the ground to the speeds: $\sin \theta(0) = c(0)/v$.
- 3 points for relating the time difference $t$ and height difference $h$ to the local angle: $\cot \theta(0) = vt/h$ (or equivalent geometric relation).
- 2 points for combining these relations to solve for the plane's velocity $v = \left( \frac{1}{\alpha^2 T_0} - \frac{t^2}{h^2} \right)^{-1/2}$.
- 3 points for correctly expressing the Mach number $M = v/c(H)$ in terms of the given parameters.

Part d (5 points):
- 2 points for identifying the condition for the boom to not reach the ground: the ray becomes horizontal at the ground, i.e., $\theta(0) = 90^\circ$.
- 1 point for stating this implies the plane's velocity equals the speed of sound at the ground, $v = c(0)$.
- 2 points for calculating the corresponding maximum Mach number $M_{\text{max}} = c(0)/c(H) = \sqrt{T_0 / (T_0 - \beta H)}$.

turns.candidate_answer:
Let \(x\) be the horizontal direction of the airplane and \(z\) be altitude. Define

\[
c_H=c(H)=\alpha\sqrt{T_0-\beta H},\qquad c_0=c(0)=\alpha\sqrt{T_0}.
\]

---

## a. Constant sound speed

For constant \(c\), the wavefronts emitted earlier are spheres centered along the plane’s past trajectory. Their envelope is a Mach cone trailing behind the plane.

In a vertical cross-section, it appears as two straight lines behind the plane, making half-angle \(\theta\) with the direction of motion, where

\[
\boxed{\sin\theta=\frac{c}{v}=\frac1M.}
\]

---

## b. Variable sound speed

Because \(T(z)=T_0-\beta z\), the sound speed is larger closer to the ground:

\[
c(z)=\alpha\sqrt{T_0-\beta z}.
\]

For the Mach envelope, the horizontal slowness is fixed:

\[
p_x=\frac{1}{v}.
\]

Thus, if \(\phi\) is the angle the sound ray makes with the horizontal,

\[
\frac{\cos\phi}{c(z)}=\frac1v.
\]

Equivalently, the local angle \(\theta(z)\) of the Mach front with the horizontal satisfies

\[
\boxed{
\sin\theta(z)=\frac{c(z)}{v}
=
\frac{1}{M}\sqrt{\frac{T_0-\beta z}{T_0-\beta H}}
}.
\]

So as the boom propagates downward, \(c(z)\) increases, and the Mach front becomes more vertical. The envelope is therefore not a straight cone: in side view, the lower branch curves and may even turn/graze before reaching the ground if \(v<c_0\).

A useful side-view expression for the lower branch at a fixed instant is

\[
x_{\text{plane}}-x(z)
=
\int_z^H
\sqrt{\frac{v^2}{c(z')^2}-1}\,dz'.
\]

---

## c. Inferring \(M\) from two vertically separated sensors

For the side-view geometry, the arrival-time difference between sensors separated by height \(h\) is

\[
t=t_2-t_1
=
\int_0^h
\sqrt{\frac{1}{c(z)^2}-\frac{1}{v^2}}\,dz.
\]

Since \(h\ll H\) and \(\beta h\ll T_0\), take \(c(z)\approx c_0=\alpha\sqrt{T_0}\) over the sensor separation:

\[
t\approx h\sqrt{\frac{1}{c_0^2}-\frac{1}{v^2}}.
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{1}{v^2}=\frac{1}{c_0^2}-\frac{t^2}{h^2}.
\]

Using \(M=v/c_H\),

\[
M
=
\frac{1}{c_H}
\left(\frac{1}{c_0^2}-\frac{t^2}{h^2}\right)^{-1/2}.
\]

Substituting \(c_0=\alpha\sqrt{T_0}\) and \(c_H=\alpha\sqrt{T_0-\beta H}\),

\[
\boxed{
M=
\left[
\left(1-\frac{\beta H}{T_0}\right)
\left(1-\alpha^2T_0\frac{t^2}{h^2}\right)
\right]^{-1/2}
}.
\]

---

## d. Mach cutoff for audibility at the ground

The boom can reach the ground only if the sound-ray condition remains real at \(z=0\):

\[
\frac{1}{c_0^2}-\frac{1}{v^2}\ge 0.
\]

Thus

\[
v\ge c_0.
\]

But \(M=v/c_H\), so the cutoff Mach number is

\[
M_{\max}=\frac{c_0}{c_H}
=
\frac{\alpha\sqrt{T_0}}{\alpha\sqrt{T_0-\beta H}}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
M_{\max}
=
\sqrt{\frac{T_0}{T_0-\beta H}}
=
\left(1-\frac{\beta H}{T_0}\right)^{-1/2}
}.
\]

For

\[
\boxed{1<M<M_{\max}},
\]

the plane is supersonic at altitude \(H\), but the boom refracts upward/turns before reaching the ground.

evidence.part_a: Candidate correctly described the straight cone geometry and the angle relation sin(theta) = 1/M.
evidence.part_b: Candidate recognized that sound speed increases with lower altitude and used Snell's law to deduce the outward-curving profile.
evidence.part_c: Candidate set up the correct integral, applied the small-height approximation, and derived the exact expression for the Mach number.
evidence.part_d: Candidate correctly identified the cutoff condition where the sound speed equals plane speed at the ground, yielding the correct maximum Mach number.

turns.question:
**Problem B3: Locked and Moded**

a. Consider two mirrors facing each other separated by a distance $L$ (a Fabry–Pérot resonator). The cavity (the space between the two mirrors) is in vacuum (index of refraction $n = 1$, no dispersion), and the mirrors have high reflectivities so that the main resonance condition is that an integer multiple of half-wavelengths fit into the cavity. A light pulse containing multiple different frequencies travels between the mirrors and interferes with itself.
i. State the condition for resonance in terms of $L$ and wavelength $\lambda$.
ii. Write down an expression for the resonant angular frequencies $\omega_m$, with $m$ counting each of the possible resonances.
iii. What is the angular frequency spacing $\Delta\omega \equiv \omega_{m+1} - \omega_m$ between adjacent angular frequencies?

b. The electric field at the antinodes of the standing waves in the resonator is a superposition of oscillations at the resonant angular frequencies and is given by:
$$E_{\text{before}}(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{+\infty} E_k \cos[(k \Delta\omega) t]$$
Now suppose we introduce a gain medium (such as a doped crystal) into the laser cavity. The gain medium completely absorbs incoming light and re-emits it over a finite range of $N$ angular frequencies centered around some angular frequency $\omega_0$, which coincides with one of the $\omega_m$ values determined above. Within this bandwidth, the gain medium amplifies and supports oscillations at all $\omega_m$ that fall within the range. (Assume $N$ is an odd number.)
Assume that each of these $N$ angular frequencies—also referred to as modes—has the same amplitude $E_0$, and that their phases are locked such that there is zero relative phase between them at $t = 0$. This condition is known as mode locking. Set their common phase so that all electric fields are expressed as cosine functions, consistent with the form of $E_{\text{before}}(t)$.
i. Write an expression for the total electric field $E_{\text{after}}(t)$ as the sum of these $N$ equally spaced angular frequencies (with zero relative phase).
ii. Show that in the limit of many angular frequencies ($\Delta\omega \ll \omega_0$, $N \gg 1$), the time-dependent electric field approximately takes the following form:
$$E_{\text{after}}(t) \approx E_0 f(\omega_0, t) \frac{\sin\left(\frac{N (\Delta\omega) t}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{(\Delta\omega) t}{2}\right)}$$
and determine the function $f(\omega_0, t)$.

c. To answer the next part of the problem, assume $N$ is odd and find the following limit when $a = \pi m$, where $m$ is an integer:
$$\lim_{x \to a} \frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}$$

d. Mode locking can dramatically increase the peak intensity $I$ of the laser output. Use the expression $I = \gamma E^2$, where $\gamma$ is a known constant, to answer the following questions.
i. Determine the total instantaneous intensity $I_{\text{after}}(t)$ of the electric field.
ii. What is the maximum possible intensity of the total field, and at what time(s) is this achieved?

e. The uncertainty principle states $\Delta x \Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}$. In optics, we are more commonly interested in the duration of the pulse rather than its spatial extent; the two are related via $\Delta x = c \Delta t$. Consider the problem of setting up a very short laser pulse. Use the uncertainty principle to estimate the required bandwidth (range of frequencies). Compare that to the relationship between pulse duration and gain bandwidth that we're achieving in this problem.
turns.official_answer:
a.
i. $\lambda = \frac{2L}{m}$
ii. $\omega_m = \frac{m \pi c}{L}$
iii. $\Delta\omega = \frac{\pi c}{L}$

b.
i. $E_{\text{after}}(t) = E_0 \sum_{k=-\frac{N-1}{2}}^{+\frac{N-1}{2}} \cos[(\omega_0 + k \Delta\omega) t]$
ii. $f(\omega_0, t) = \cos(\omega_0 t)$

c. $N$

d.
i. $I_{\text{after}}(t) = \gamma \left[ E_0 \cos(\omega_0 t) \frac{\sin\left(\frac{N (\Delta\omega) t}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{(\Delta\omega) t}{2}\right)} \right]^2$
ii. $I_{\text{max}} = \gamma (N E_0)^2$, achieved at $t = \frac{2\pi m}{\Delta\omega}$ for integer $m$.

e. The uncertainty principle gives $\Delta t \Delta\omega \ge 1$. In our setup, the bandwidth is $N\Delta\omega$, and the pulse duration is $t \sim \frac{1}{N\Delta\omega}$, which exactly matches the relationship in the uncertainty principle.

**Part b (7 points)**

- 2 points for correctly applying the trigonometric identity to sum the series.

- 2 points for determining the correct maximum possible intensity $I_{\text{max}} = \gamma (N E_0)^2$.

## a. Fabry–Pérot resonances

### i. Resonance condition

An integer number of half-wavelengths must fit inside the cavity:

\[
L=\frac{m\lambda}{2},
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\boxed{2L=m\lambda}
\]

for positive integer \(m\).

### ii. Resonant angular frequencies

Since \(\lambda_m=2L/m\),

\[
f_m=\frac{c}{\lambda_m}=\frac{mc}{2L}.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{\omega_m=2\pi f_m=\frac{m\pi c}{L}}
\]

for \(m=1,2,3,\dots\).

### iii. Angular frequency spacing

\[
\Delta\omega=\omega_{m+1}-\omega_m
=\frac{(m+1)\pi c}{L}-\frac{m\pi c}{L}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{\Delta\omega=\frac{\pi c}{L}}.
\]

---

## b. Mode-locked electric field

Let \(N\) be odd, and define

\[
K=\frac{N-1}{2}.
\]

The supported modes are centered around \(\omega_0\), so their angular frequencies are

\[
\omega_0+k\Delta\omega,
\qquad
k=-K,-K+1,\dots,K.
\]

### i. Total electric field

With equal amplitude \(E_0\) and zero relative phase at \(t=0\),

\[
\boxed{
E_{\text{after}}(t)
=
E_0\sum_{k=-K}^{K}
\cos\left[(\omega_0+k\Delta\omega)t\right]
}
\]

where \(K=(N-1)/2\).

### ii. Envelope form

Use

\[
\cos[(\omega_0+k\Delta\omega)t]
=
\cos(\omega_0 t)\cos(k\Delta\omega t)
-
\sin(\omega_0 t)\sin(k\Delta\omega t).
\]

Because the sum is symmetric about \(k=0\), the sine terms cancel. Thus

\[
E_{\text{after}}(t)
=
E_0\cos(\omega_0 t)
\sum_{k=-K}^{K}\cos(k\Delta\omega t).
\]

The finite cosine sum gives

\[
\sum_{k=-K}^{K}\cos(kx)
=
\frac{\sin(Nx/2)}{\sin(x/2)}.
\]

With \(x=\Delta\omega t\),

\[
\boxed{
E_{\text{after}}(t)
=
E_0\cos(\omega_0 t)
\frac{\sin\left(\frac{N\Delta\omega t}{2}\right)}
{\sin\left(\frac{\Delta\omega t}{2}\right)}
}
\]

So in the requested form,

\[
\boxed{f(\omega_0,t)=\cos(\omega_0 t)}.
\]

The factor \(\cos(\omega_0 t)\) is the fast carrier oscillation, while the sine ratio is the slowly varying pulse envelope.

---

## c. Limit of \(\sin(Nx)/\sin x\)

Let \(a=\pi m\), where \(m\) is an integer. Then both numerator and denominator vanish, so use L’Hôpital’s rule:

\[
\lim_{x\to a}\frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}
=
\lim_{x\to a}\frac{N\cos(Nx)}{\cos x}.
\]

Thus

\[
\lim_{x\to \pi m}\frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}
=
N\frac{\cos(N\pi m)}{\cos(\pi m)}.
\]

Since \(N\) is odd,

\[
\cos(N\pi m)=(-1)^{Nm}=(-1)^m=\cos(\pi m).
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\lim_{x\to \pi m}\frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}=N
}
\]

for odd \(N\).

---

## d. Intensity of the mode-locked field

### i. Instantaneous intensity

Using \(I=\gamma E^2\),

\[
\boxed{
I_{\text{after}}(t)
=
\gamma E_0^2
\cos^2(\omega_0 t)
\left[
\frac{\sin\left(\frac{N\Delta\omega t}{2}\right)}
{\sin\left(\frac{\Delta\omega t}{2}\right)}
\right]^2
}
\]

### ii. Maximum intensity

The electric field is largest when all \(N\) modes are in phase. At those times,

\[
E_{\max}=NE_0.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
I_{\max}=\gamma N^2E_0^2
}
\]

This occurs when

\[
\frac{\Delta\omega t}{2}=\pi q,
\]

so

\[
\boxed{
t=\frac{2\pi q}{\Delta\omega}
}
\]

for integer \(q\). Since \(\Delta\omega=\pi c/L\),

\[
\boxed{
t=\frac{2L}{c}q
}
\]

which is every cavity round-trip time.

---

## e. Bandwidth and pulse duration

For a photon,

\[
p=\frac{\hbar\omega}{c},
\]

so

\[
\Delta p=\frac{\hbar\,\Delta\omega_{\text{bw}}}{c}.
\]

Using \(\Delta x=c\Delta t\), the uncertainty principle gives

\[
\Delta x\Delta p\gtrsim \frac{\hbar}{2}.
\]

Thus

\[
(c\Delta t)\left(\frac{\hbar\Delta\omega_{\text{bw}}}{c}\right)
\gtrsim \frac{\hbar}{2},
\]

so

\[
\boxed{
\Delta t\,\Delta\omega_{\text{bw}}\gtrsim \frac12
}
\]

up to order-one numerical factors. Therefore, producing a short pulse requires a large frequency bandwidth:

\[
\boxed{
\Delta\omega_{\text{bw}}\sim \frac{1}{\Delta t}.
}
\]

In the mode-locked cavity, the total gain bandwidth is roughly

\[
\Delta\omega_{\text{bw}}\sim N\Delta\omega.
\]

The pulse envelope has its first zeros when

\[
\frac{N\Delta\omega t}{2}=\pm \pi,
\]

so the pulse duration is of order

\[
\Delta t\sim \frac{1}{N\Delta\omega}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\Delta t\sim \frac{1}{\Delta\omega_{\text{bw}}}
}
\]

up to numerical constants. This agrees with the uncertainty-principle estimate: shorter laser pulses require broader gain bandwidths.
